Task 1: Synthesis Divergence
Framing the complexity, the tools brought to the problem, and the boundaries of the knowledge domain
ETSII | UPM — AI for Management
1. Object and Approach
The document is organised in five parts: (1) how each paper frames the complexity of the problem; (2) which tools are brought to bear on it and why; (3) where the boundaries of the knowledge domain lie; (4) extracted metadata for the corpus; and (5) the full reference list, followed by notes and scope caveats.
Papers are referred to by the identifiers assigned in Task 2 and repeated in the metadata table of Section 5.
2. Framing the Complexity
The five papers face problems that are all computationally hard, but they locate the hardness in different places. Naming that location explains almost every subsequent methodological choice.
2.1 Four distinct sources of difficulty
2.2 The shared move: transfer the hardness elsewhere
Despite the divergence, every paper performs the same manoeuvre: it accepts an irreducible hardness and displaces the cost to a stage where it can be paid more cheaply.
P1 pays offline in analysis: derive the optimal control law by Pontryagin's minimum principle, prove concavity, and the online scheduling becomes polynomial.
P2 pays in surrogate training: fit a support vector regression to approximate simulated fitness, freeing search effort for the solution space.
P3 pays in forecasting: build the grey-plus-neural release-time model offline so that online rescheduling starts from an informed prior and a quantified error distribution.
P5 pays in reinforcement learning: run ALADIN offline on sampled scenarios, learn the consensus-variable dynamics with SAC, and obtain online decisions roughly 100 times faster than a commercial solver.
P4 pays in representation: precompute explanatory artefacts (decision trees, contribution diagrams) that shift the interpretive burden off the user.
The divergence is therefore not about whether to displace complexity but about the currency in which it is paid: mathematical proof (P1), statistical learning (P2, P5), predictive modelling (P3), or visual representation (P4).
3. The Tools Brought to the Problem
3.1 Tool inventory by paper
3.2 Divergence on three shared questions
(a) How is uncertainty represented?
P2 assumes known parametric distributions — exponential breakdown time and exponential maintenance duration, justified by historical statistics.
P3 refuses distributional assumptions and replaces them with a forecasting model plus an empirical accuracy structure (global accuracy and a local accuracy matrix over binned error intervals).
P5 fits empirical probability densities per medium, finding normal shapes for BFG, LDG and electricity but bimodal mixtures for steam and COG, and positions its output explicitly between robust optimisation (too conservative) and stochastic optimisation (too absolute).
P1 and P4 are deterministic; P1 acknowledges that its control may not be exactly optimal in practice and proposes a simple feedback fallback near the operating point.
These are three incompatible epistemologies of the same object. P2 trusts the distribution, P3 trusts the predictor, P5 trusts the data. No paper benchmarks one against the others.
(b) How is non-convexity or intractability circumvented?
P1 proves the obstacle away: concavity of the idle energy function is established as a theorem, which legitimises the polynomial algorithm.
P3 removes it by construction: once the chromosome fixes all binary variables, the residual model is linear and solvable exactly.
P5 relaxes it: piecewise linearisation of the Weymouth equation and SOCP relaxation of the power flow, then a distributed Newton-type method, then learning to imitate that method.
P2 and P4 do not confront convexity at all; they work in a purely combinatorial space where the notion does not apply.
(c) What counts as a good solution?
P1: provable optimality plus measured energy savings against transition-graph baselines with one or two standby modes.
P2: dominance in Pareto terms, assessed by inverted generational distance and hyper-volume, plus lower rescheduling cost and match-up time on plant data.
P3: statistically significant improvement in MSM and RM against PIDE and IABC under equal CPU budgets, tested by Wilcoxon signed-rank.
P4: perceived understandability scored 1–10 by five employees, plus coverage of a nine-item requirements checklist.
P5: economic cost, computation time, stability across 100+ simulations, and a "price of robustness" bounded at 1.18 % above the ideal cost.
The evaluative criteria are close to incommensurable. P4 is the only paper whose success metric is human rather than numerical, which is exactly why it cannot be ranked against the others.
4. Boundaries of the Knowledge Domain
The corpus defines a domain that can be stated positively and negatively.
4.1 What is inside the boundary
Application sector: heavy, energy-intensive discrete manufacturing — steelmaking, continuous casting, ingot rolling, steel hardening, glass tempering by analogy, with one excursion into ubiquitous 3D-printing manufacturing (P4).
Decision horizon: operational and tactical. Scheduling horizons of hours to a working week; energy dispatch in 15-minute intervals over a 2-hour cycle. No strategic or capacity-planning decisions.
Decision objects: start times, job sequences, resource/compression allocation, machine-to-job assignment, equipment on/off and set-point levels, gasholder levels.
Disturbance classes: machine breakdown, release-time deviation, energy supply/demand fluctuation, deterioration through waiting.
Methodological families: exact graph/DP algorithms, optimal control, mixed-integer and chance-constrained programming, evolutionary and memetic algorithms, surrogate modelling, deep reinforcement learning, distributed optimisation, XAI.
Validation regime: real industrial data from named plants, complemented by synthetic instance generators.
4.2 What lies outside the boundary
Supply chain and multi-plant coordination. Every paper stops at the plant gate; logistics, inventory and customer-order dynamics are exogenous.
Human and organisational factors, except as a reception problem in P4. Operator workload, shift structure, ergonomics and safety are absent.
Environmental objectives as such. Energy is minimised for cost, not for emissions; carbon accounting appears only marginally (zero gas emission is noted as a by-product in P5).
Quality outcomes. Product quality is treated as a constraint to be respected (fixed processing temperature, fixed processing time) rather than as a decision variable.
Maintenance policy design. Maintenance appears only as a stochastic interruption (P2) or an immediate repair; preventive maintenance optimisation is cited but not modelled.
Market and price uncertainty. Time-of-use electricity tariffs are exogenous and known in P5; no paper treats price as stochastic.
Combined production–energy decision-making. Scheduling (P1–P4) and energy dispatch (P5) remain formally disjoint even though they govern the same equipment.
Non-steel process industries, general manufacturing, semiconductor fabs and service operations, which appear only as citations for method transfer.
4.3 Boundary conditions and assumptions that hold the domain together
Equipment behaviour is stationary and identifiable over the horizon considered (constant ambient temperature in P1; fixed production process and core equipment in P5).
The sequence or the batch allocation is at least partially predetermined (fixed task order in P1; predetermined casting sequence and machine allocation in the last stage in P3).
Historical data are available in sufficient volume and quality to fit distributions or forecasting models (one year at one-minute resolution in P5; 6 896 jobs over 57 days in P3).
The objective is separable into cost terms with tunable penalty coefficients, so that multi-criteria problems can be scalarised or Pareto-ranked.
5. Metadata Extraction
5.1 Bibliographic metadata
5.2 Content metadata
5.3 Derived metadata (assigned during this review)
6. Full Reference List
6.1 Primary corpus

6.2 Key secondary works cited within the corpus
The following are the works most frequently invoked across the five papers as the methodological or empirical foundations of the domain. They are listed because they mark the intellectual perimeter within which the corpus operates.
Aghelinejad, M., Ouazene, Y., & Yalaoui, A. (2019). Complexity analysis of energy-efficient single machine scheduling problems. Operations Research Perspectives, 6, 100105. [Cited by P1 as the nearest polynomial-time comparator.]

Chee Chook, K., & Tan, A. H. (2007). Identification of an electric resistance furnace. IEEE Transactions on Instrumentation and Measurement, 56, 2262–2270. [Source of the bilinear furnace model adopted in P1.]
Deb, K., Pratap, A., Agarwal, S., & Meyarivan, T. (2002). A fast and elitist multiobjective genetic algorithm: NSGA-II. IEEE Transactions on Evolutionary Computation, 6, 182–197. [Engine of P2.]
Garey, M., & Johnson, D. (1977). Two-processor scheduling with start-times and deadlines. SIAM Journal on Computing, 6(3), 416–426. [NP-hardness result underpinning the fixed-order assumption in P1.]
Gerards, M. E. T., & Kuper, J. (2013). Optimal DPM and DVFS for frame-based real-time systems. ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization, 9(4), 41:1–41:23. [Origin of the concave idle energy function concept extended by P1.]
Haarnoja, T., et al. (2018). Soft actor-critic algorithms and applications. arXiv:1812.05905. [Algorithmic basis of the SAC agent in P5.]
Holzinger, A., Saranti, A., Molnar, C., Biecek, P., & Samek, W. (2022). Explainable AI methods — A brief overview. Lecture Notes in Artificial Intelligence, 13200, 13–38. [Taxonomy used by P4 to position its contribution.]
Jin, Y. (2005). A comprehensive survey of fitness approximation in evolutionary computation. Soft Computing, 9(1), 3–12. [Rationale for surrogate-assisted search in P2.]
Mouzon, G., Yildirim, M., & Twomey, J. (2007). Operational methods for minimization of energy consumption of manufacturing equipment. International Journal of Production Research, 45, 4247–4271. [Origin of the machine-mode / transition-graph paradigm that P1 criticises.]
Pezzella, F., Morganti, G., & Ciaschetti, G. (2008). A genetic algorithm for the flexible job-shop scheduling problem. Computers & Operations Research, 35(10), 3202–3212. [Case study reused by P4.]
Ribeiro, M. T., Singh, S., & Guestrin, C. (2016). "Why should I trust you?" Explaining the predictions of any classifier. Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGKDD, 1135–1144. [LIME philosophy invoked and found insufficient by P4.]
Tang, L., Zhao, Y., & Liu, J. (2014). An improved differential evolution algorithm for practical dynamic scheduling in steelmaking-continuous casting production. IEEE Transactions on Evolutionary Computation, 18, 209–225. [PIDE baseline in P3.]
Zhai, J., et al. (2022). Distributed optimal power flow for VSC-MTDC meshed AC/DC grids using ALADIN. IEEE Transactions on Power Systems, 37(6), 4861–4873. [ALADIN reference implementation used in P5.]
Zitzler, E., & Thiele, L. (1998). Multiobjective optimization using evolutionary algorithms — A comparative case study. PPSN V, LNCS 1498, 292–301. [Hyper-volume metric used in P2.]
7. Notes and Scope Caveats
7.1 Caveats on the corpus
Sample size. Five papers cannot characterise a research field. The corpus is a purposive, not a systematic, sample: no database query, inclusion protocol or PRISMA-style screening was applied, so selection bias cannot be estimated.
Temporal spread. Publication years run from 2019 (with P2 first published online in 2017) to 2025. Methods that were state of the art in the earlier papers — SVR surrogates, differential evolution baselines — are compared implicitly against much more recent DRL work. Apparent superiority of later papers partly reflects publication date, not method quality.
Geographic and institutional concentration. Three of the five papers originate from Chinese institutions working with Chinese steel plants; one is Czech, one Taiwanese. Findings about plant practice, tariff structures and manual scheduling habits may not transfer to other industrial cultures.
No shared benchmark. Each paper validates on its own instances against its own baselines. No two papers can be compared on a common dataset, so relative performance claims made here are qualitative only.
Self-reported results. All performance figures are the authors' own; none has been independently replicated in this review. P5's energy dataset is publicly available, but the others are not, and P4 explicitly states that its data cannot be shared.
7.2 Caveats on the analysis performed
Edge weights in the Task 2 network are analyst-assigned by counting shared dimensions across the four domains of the topic tree. They are ordinal and reproducible only given the same tree; a different decomposition would give a different graph.
The "derived metadata" of Section 5.3 (uncertainty stance, interpretability, role in corpus) are interpretive labels, not properties claimed by the authors.
Terminological drift is present and has been smoothed over. "Robustness" means insensitivity of rescheduling cost in P2, low RM across rescheduling events in P3, and bounded cost excess under supply/demand fluctuation in P5. These are not the same quantity; treating them as one concept in Section 3.2 is an analytical convenience.
Likewise "uncertainty" covers a stochastic process (P2), a forecast residual (P3) and a sampling distribution (P5). The comparison is conceptual, not formal.
Only the full texts supplied were analysed. Supplementary material, appendices and code repositories referenced by the authors were not consulted.
7.3 Caveats on generalisation
P1's polynomial result is conditional on two assumptions that are strong in practice: a fixed task order and a concave idle energy function. The authors themselves leave open whether the problem stays polynomial for an arbitrary non-concave function.
P2's flexibility measure relies on power coefficients tuned on a ten-job instance and then reused at n = 100; the stability of that transfer is not established.
P3 demonstrates that forecasting accuracy degrades performance when noise exceeds roughly ±12–18 minutes, which bounds the operating envelope of the approach and requires periodic model retraining.
P4's effectiveness evidence rests on five employees scoring understandability on a 1–10 scale, with the authors conceding substantial room for improvement. This is indicative, not evidential.
P5's speed advantage is measured against Gurobi 10.0.2 on a desktop i5 with 16 GB RAM and a network simplified to 100 PWL segments; scaling claims beyond that configuration are extrapolations.
7.4 Note on citation convention
Throughout this document, statements attributed to a paper paraphrase that paper's own claims and are labelled with the corresponding identifier. Where a numerical value is quoted it is taken directly from the paper's reported results. No claim in Sections 2 to 4 should be read as an independent empirical finding of this review.
Document prepared as deliverable for Task 3 — Synthesis Divergence. Companion to the Task 2 topographical mapping.
ID | Where the difficulty sits | Framing adopted
P1 | Combinatorial, but tamed | The underlying single-machine problem with release times and deadlines is NP-hard, so the authors fix the task order and prove that, if the idle energy function is concave, block-form schedules dominate and the problem reduces to a shortest path in a DAG solvable in O(n³). Complexity is deliberately relocated into the modelling of machine dynamics, not the search.
P2 | Stochastic and evaluative | The combinatorial sequencing is hard, but the binding constraint is the cost of evaluating a candidate: robustness and stability must be estimated by simulating many breakdown scenarios. Complexity is framed as an evaluation-budget problem.
P3 | Epistemic and dynamic | The hybrid flow shop with batching is NP-hard, yet the authors frame the real difficulty as not knowing when jobs arrive. Uncertainty in release times triggers high-frequency rescheduling that destabilises production; complexity is framed as forecast error propagating into schedule instability.
P4 | Cognitive, not computational | P4 accepts the NP-hardness as settled (2.64 × 10⁹ permutations in the case study) and reframes the problem: the obstacle to deploying GA is that shop-floor personnel cannot understand or trust it. Complexity is framed as an explanation gap.
P5 | Non-convex and high-dimensional | The energy system is non-convex (Weymouth gas flow, steam heat transfer, power flow) and carries a very large state space across five energy media. Complexity is framed jointly as non-convexity plus the curse of dimensionality in learning.
ID | Primary tool | Supporting tools | Justification given
P1 | Graph reduction to shortest path (dynamic programming) | Pontryagin minimum principle; bilinear system identification by least squares; Filippov/Carathéodory solutions for discontinuous ODEs | Guarantees optimality and a complexity independent of the scheduling horizon length |H|, unlike discretised ILP models whose size grows with the horizon.
P2 | NSGA-II (elitist non-dominated sorting GA) | Support vector regression surrogate with RBF kernel; probabilistic sequencing strategy using downtime probability; scenario-based Monte Carlo evaluation | A population method returns the whole Pareto front in one run; the surrogate cuts the cost of simulation-based fitness; the sequencing strategy injects domain knowledge into the search.
P3 | Chance-constrained programming solved by Monte Carlo + memetic GA (GALS) | NNGR forecasting (GM(1,1) + residual GM(1,1) + ANN sign estimation); random-key encoding; LP decoding via CPLEX/Gurobi; local search LS1–LS4 | The distribution of release times cannot be assumed, so forecasting accuracy substitutes for it as the confidence level; fixing discrete variables leaves an LP that decodes almost instantly.
P4 | Decision-tree-based interpretation | Dynamic transition and contribution diagrams (radar-chart based); improved bar charts with colour management and annotation | Decision trees are simple enough to explain not only GA but also other XAI tools; standard input–output fitting methods (LIME, SHAP, CART) fail because there is no stable mapping from feasible to optimal solutions in a GA.
P5 | Two-stage data-driven DRL (2S-DSAC) | ALADIN for non-convex distributed optimisation; SAC with entropy maximisation; PWL and SOCP relaxations; fuzzy c-means clustering; probability models of energy media | ALADIN achieves local quadratic convergence on non-convex problems where ADMM may not converge; recasting consensus-variable iteration as an MDP avoids defining every decision variable as a state.

Task 2: Topographical Mapping
Hierarchical topic tree and cross-reference network of the reviewed corpus
ETSII | UPM — AI for Management
1. Purpose and Method
This document delivers the topographical mapping of the five-paper corpus. Two complementary artefacts are produced. First, a hierarchical topic tree that decomposes the corpus into domains, sub-domains and leaf concepts. Second, a cross-reference network graph that links the papers through shared constructs, methods and application contexts. The rationale is that the tree shows what is discussed, while the graph shows where knowledge is concentrated and where it is isolated, revealing hidden structural relationships that a paper-by-paper reading cannot expose.
Corpus under analysis:
2. Hierarchical Topic Tree
The corpus organises itself around one root problem — decision-making under uncertainty in energy-intensive discrete manufacturing (steel and heat-intensive processes) — which branches into four first-level domains.
Root: Optimisation of production and energy decisions in steel / heat-intensive manufacturing
D1. Problem Formulation (What is optimised)
D1.1 Scheduling problems
Single-machine with release times, deadlines and fixed order — 1|rj, d̃j, fixed order|ΣE (P1)
Single-machine proactive scheduling with controllable processing times and deterioration (P2)
Hybrid flow shop / steelmaking–continuous casting (SCC) with batching in the last stage (P3)
Flexible job shop / flexible flow shop makespan minimisation (P4)
D1.2 Energy allocation problems
Idle energy consumption minimisation over idle periods (P1)
Multi-medium energy dispatch: by-product gases (BFG, COG, LDG), steam, electricity (P5)
D1.3 Objective structures
Single objective: idle energy (P1); economic operating cost (P5)
Bi-objective / Pareto: robustness E(f) vs. stability Var(f) (P2)
Weighted multi-objective: waiting time, makespan, cast breaks, start-time deviation (P3)
Makespan as canonical target for explanation (P4)
D2. Uncertainty and Robustness (How disturbance is handled)
D2.1 Sources of uncertainty
Stochastic machine breakdown and maintenance duration (P2)
Uncertain job release times / hot-metal ladle arrival (P3)
Energy supply and demand fluctuation (P5)
Deterministic setting — no explicit uncertainty modelled (P1, P4)
D2.2 Coping strategies
Proactive / predictive scheduling with buffering vs. non-buffering (P2)
Match-up rescheduling via controllable processing times (P2)
Reactive dispatching rules and pure rescheduling (discussed and rejected in P3)
Forecast-informed robust scheduling: NNGR grey model + ANN sign estimation (P3)
Chance-constrained programming with confidence level from forecasting accuracy (P3)
Stochastic vs. robust vs. distributionally robust optimisation (surveyed and positioned in P5)
Rolling-horizon execution: only the first control action is applied (P3, P5)
D2.3 Robustness / stability metrics
Mean and variance of rescheduling cost; match-up time cost + resource cost (P2)
MSM (mean scheduling measure) and RM (robustness measure) (P3)
Price of robustness vs. ideal cost under fluctuation ratios (P5)
D3. Solution Methods (How the problem is solved)
D3.1 Exact and polynomial-time methods
Reduction to shortest path in a directed acyclic energy graph, O(n³) (P1)
Block-form dominance argument under a concave idle energy function (P1)
Linear programming decoding of fixed discrete variables (P3)
Piecewise linearisation (PWL) and second-order cone programming (SOCP) relaxations (P5)
D3.2 Metaheuristics and evolutionary computation
NSGA-II as multi-objective engine (P2)
Genetic algorithm with local search — memetic GALS (P3)
Genetic algorithms: selection, crossover, mutation as the object of explanation (P4)
Related families cited as extensions: ACO, PSO, ABC (P4)
D3.3 Surrogate and learning-assisted search
Support vector regression surrogate replacing simulation-based fitness (P2)
Problem-specific probabilistic sequencing strategy using downtime probability (P2)
Deep reinforcement learning: SAC, DDPG, PER-SAC (P5)
Consensus-variable iteration recast as a Markov Decision Process (P5)
D3.4 Distributed and decomposition schemes
Decomposition into (i) idle energy function determination and (ii) optimal scheduling (P1)
ALADIN, ADMM, Prox-JADMM for non-convex distributed optimisation (P5)
D3.5 Simulation and sampling
Scenario-based evaluation of breakdown scenarios (P2)
Monte Carlo simulation to solve the chance-constrained model (P3)
Monte Carlo sampling for robustness assessment (P5)
D4. Modelling, Data and Interpretability (What supports the model)
D4.1 Physical / process models
Bilinear furnace dynamics identified by least squares; Pontryagin minimum principle for optimal control (P1)
Weymouth equation for gas pipeline flow; steam heat-transfer equations; DistFlow power model (P5)
Deterioration effect: processing time as a non-decreasing function of start/waiting time (P2)
D4.2 Data-driven models
Grey GM(1,1) + residual GM(1,1) + ANN sign estimation (NNGR) for release times (P3)
Probability density modelling of energy media, including bimodal mixtures (P5)
Fuzzy c-means clustering for online correction of forecasts (P5)
D4.3 Explainability and human acceptance
Decision-tree-based interpretation of selection, crossover and mutation (P4)
Dynamic transition and contribution diagrams based on radar charts (P4)
Improved bar charts: common expressions, colour management, annotation (P4)
Requirements framework for an adequate XAI technique in scheduling (P4)
D4.4 Validation
Real industrial case: Škoda Auto vacuum hardening furnace (P1)
Practical data from a large Chinese steel company, 20 ingots (P2)
Panzhihua Iron and Steel, 6 896 jobs over 57 days (P3)
Flexible job shop from literature + ubiquitous manufacturing 3D-printing cell (P4)
Chinese steel enterprise, one year of one-minute energy data (P5)
3. Cross-Reference Network Graph
The network is defined as an undirected weighted graph G = (V, E) where V is the set of five papers and each edge weight is the number of shared conceptual dimensions. Edges are derived from co-occurrence across the four domains of the topic tree, not from bibliographic citation, since the five papers do not cite one another.
3.1 Adjacency Matrix (edge weight = number of shared dimensions)
Degree strength: P3 = 14, P5 = 13, P2 = 13, P4 = 9, P1 = 9. P3 and P5 act as hubs; P1 and P4 are peripheral in different ways — P1 is methodologically isolated, P4 is thematically transversal but empirically detached.
3.2 Edge Descriptions
3.3 Network Diagram (textual rendering)
P2 ═════ P3        (strongest edge: steel + uncertainty + GA)
║    ╳    ║
║  ╱   ╲  ║
P4       P5 ═════ P1   (energy + physics-based models)
Legend: ═ strong edge (4–5), ─ / ╳ medium edge (3), thin or absent ties elsewhere. P4 connects to the GA cluster (P2, P3) but not to the energy cluster (P1, P5); P1 connects to the energy cluster only.
4. Concentrations of Knowledge
Four dense regions emerge where three or more papers converge.
5. Isolated Knowledge and Structural Gaps
Explainability is a singleton. Only P4 addresses interpretability. P2, P3 and P5 deploy black-box surrogates (SVR), deep networks (SAC/DDPG) and hybrid metaheuristics in industrial settings without any mechanism for operator trust — precisely the acceptance problem P4 diagnoses. This is the largest structural hole in the corpus.
Polynomial-time optimality is a singleton. Only P1 proves tractability and optimality; every other paper accepts heuristic or approximate solutions. The concavity condition exploited in P1 is never tested against the energy functions implied in P5, although both concern idle/standby energy in heat-intensive equipment.
Deterioration effects are isolated in P2. The idea that waiting degrades processing time (steel ingots cooling) appears nowhere else, even though P3 models the same physical plant family and P1 models exactly the thermal dynamics that would cause it.
Optimal control theory is isolated in P1. Pontryagin's minimum principle and the derivation of a switching-time control law have no counterpart, despite P5 solving a control-adjacent dispatch problem over the same class of equipment.
Forecasting of exogenous inputs is isolated in P3. Grey prediction with neural residual correction is unique; P5 instead fits static probability densities, and P2 assumes known exponential distributions. No paper compares these three representations of the same epistemic object.
Distributed/decentralised optimisation is isolated in P5. ALADIN, ADMM and consensus variables appear nowhere else, although the block structure exploited in P1 (blocks of tasks separated by idle periods) is structurally analogous.
No paper couples production scheduling with energy dispatch. P1–P4 schedule jobs; P5 dispatches energy. The physical plant is the same steel works, and the two decisions are coupled through equipment state, yet no edge in the graph carries this integration.
6. Hidden Structural Relationships
The mapping exposes three relationships that are not visible from the abstracts.
A decomposition isomorphism. P1 splits the problem into "determine the energy function" plus "schedule optimally". P3 splits it into "forecast release times offline" plus "reschedule robustly online". P5 splits it into "learn consensus dynamics offline" plus "correct by clustering online". Three papers, three domains, one architectural pattern: push the expensive, physics- or data-heavy computation offline and leave a cheap decision rule online. None of the three recognises the pattern in the others.
A convexity/tractability axis running orthogonal to the topic tree. P1 secures polynomial time by proving concavity of the idle energy function; P5 confronts non-convexity head-on (Weymouth equation, power flow) and escapes via PWL, SOCP and ALADIN; P3 escapes by fixing discrete variables so the residual problem becomes an LP. The corpus therefore contains three distinct strategies for the same underlying obstacle — non-convexity — which the topic tree files under separate branches.
A surrogate-substitution chain. P2 replaces expensive simulation with SVR; P5 replaces an expensive mechanistic solver (ALADIN) with a trained SAC policy; P4 argues that any such replacement creates an explanation debt. Read in sequence, P2 → P5 → P4 forms a latent argument: the more aggressively optimisation is surrogated for speed, the more urgently XAI is required. No individual paper makes this argument; it is a property of the network.
7. Implications for Task 3
The mapping identifies the sub-topics where synthesis divergence is most likely to be productive: (i) representation of uncertainty — known distribution (P2) vs. forecast-plus-error-statistics (P3) vs. empirical density (P5); (ii) treatment of non-convexity — prove it away (P1) vs. relax it (P5) vs. fix variables around it (P3); (iii) the speed–transparency trade-off, where the surrogate-substitution chain (P2, P5) stands in direct tension with the interpretability requirements of P4.
